title: Optimizing Water Use in Singapore Data Centres
abstract: A practical look at how Singapore's data centres can cut water use without sacrificing reliability, based on real operating data and a bit of arithmetic.
body:
## Introduction

I spent last week at a workshop in Singapore, where the topic was water use in data centres. As an energy-systems professor, I usually focus on electricity, but water is becoming a critical constraint. Singapore imports about 40% of its water from Malaysia, and the rest comes from desalination and NEWater. Data centres are thirsty: they use water for cooling, and with the push for AI, demand is rising. In this post, I want to walk through the arithmetic of water use and share some optimization strategies that I've seen work.

## The Water-Energy Nexus in Cooling

Most data centres in Singapore use chilled water systems. The cooling tower evaporates water to reject heat. The amount of water evaporated depends on the heat load and the efficiency of the cooling system. A typical rule of thumb is that for every kilowatt-hour of IT load, you need about 1.5 to 2.5 liters of water for cooling, depending on the climate and the cooling system design. Let's do the math: a 10 MW data centre running at 80% utilization has an IT load of 8 MW. Over a day, that's 8,000 kW * 24 h = 192,000 kWh. At 2 liters per kWh, that's 384,000 liters, or 384 cubic meters per day. That's a lot of water. And that's just for cooling; there's also water for humidification and other uses.

But not all that water is consumed. Some is lost to evaporation, some is blown down to control dissolved solids, and some is discharged. The evaporation loss is the main consumptive use. The blowdown can be minimized with proper water treatment. So the actual water footprint can be reduced.

## Strategies for Reducing Water Use

There are several ways to reduce water use in data centres. First, increase the cooling tower cycles of concentration. This means allowing the water to have higher dissolved solids before blowdown. By optimizing water treatment, you can reduce blowdown significantly. For example, if you increase cycles from 3 to 6, you can cut blowdown by half. That saves water and also reduces chemical use.

Second, use alternative cooling technologies. Air-side economizers can reduce water use, but in Singapore's humid climate, they are less effective. However, indirect evaporative cooling can be a good compromise. Another option is to use seawater cooling, but that requires proximity to the coast and careful environmental impact assessment.

Third, recover water from other sources. For instance, condensate from air handling units can be collected and used as makeup water. In a typical data centre, condensate can provide 5-10% of makeup water needs. Also, treated wastewater from NEWater can be used for cooling, but that requires a separate pipeline.

Fourth, optimize the operation of the cooling system. For example, raise the chilled water supply temperature. For every degree Celsius increase, you can save about 2-3% of cooling energy, and also reduce water evaporation because the cooling tower operates more efficiently. But you need to ensure that the IT equipment can tolerate higher temperatures. ASHRAE guidelines allow up to 27°C for inlet air in some classes.

## Case Study: A Singapore Data Centre

Let me share a case study from a data centre I visited in Singapore. It's a 5 MW facility with a mix of cloud and enterprise customers. They implemented a few measures: they increased cycles of concentration from 3 to 5, installed a condensate recovery system, and raised the chilled water supply temperature from 7°C to 10°C. The results were impressive. Water consumption dropped from 1.8 liters per kWh to 1.2 liters per kWh. That's a 33% reduction. In absolute terms, for a 5 MW facility at 70% utilization, IT load is 3.5 MW. Daily energy is 3,500 kW * 24 = 84,000 kWh. Water use before: 84,000 * 1.8 = 151,200 liters per day. After: 84,000 * 1.2 = 100,800 liters per day. Savings: 50,400 liters per day, or about 18.4 million liters per year. That's enough to fill about 7 Olympic-sized swimming pools. The payback period for the upgrades was under two years, based on water and energy savings.

## The Role of Policy and Standards

Singapore's government has been proactive. The Public Utilities Board (PUB) has introduced water efficiency requirements for data centres. The Building and Construction Authority (BCA) has a Green Mark scheme that awards points for water efficiency. Also, the Singapore Standard SS 530 provides guidelines for energy and water efficiency in data centres. These policies are pushing operators to adopt best practices. However, there is still room for improvement. Many older data centres have not been retrofitted. I think mandatory water reporting would help, similar to what we have for energy.

## Conclusion

Optimizing water use in Singapore data centres is not just an environmental imperative; it's a business one. Water is becoming scarcer and more expensive. By applying simple measures like increasing cycles of concentration, recovering condensate, and optimizing cooling system operation, operators can significantly reduce their water footprint. The arithmetic shows that the savings can be substantial. As a professor, I encourage my students to think about the water-energy nexus. It's all connected. In future posts, I'll explore how AI can help optimize cooling systems in real time. For now, I hope this gives you a practical starting point.

Note: This article is based on fictional data and scenarios for illustrative purposes. Real-world results may vary.
